title: Harvey Raises at $11 Billion Valuation to Scale Agents Across Law Firms and Enterprises
author: Harvey Team · Ashley Capoot (CNBC) · Julie Bort (TechCrunch)

dom.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source accepts that Harvey’s rapid revenue, adoption and financing demonstrate strong vertical-AI traction while not establishing legal performance or durable leadership. It materially extends the cluster with March 2026 evidence on agent deployment, embedded legal engineering and application-layer implementation, while treating long-term dominance as investor prediction rather than proof.
qs: Harvey is showing that AI startups focused on specific industries are able to get traction even as OpenAI and Anthropic continue expanding their offerings.
Grady said that because model capabilities are improving so quickly, trying to apply them in real-world situations is a bigger undertaking than it has been for software companies in the past.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source supports Harvey as a meaningful test case for specialist legal-AI durability, citing financing momentum, reported adoption and traction despite foundation-model expansion. It remains cautious: these indicators do not establish product effectiveness or durable advantage, and applying rapidly improving models remains operationally demanding.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: The source directly supports Harvey’s infrastructure strategy through company-reported deployment of agent-led workflows, customer-facing legal engineering and substantial adoption across law firms and in-house teams. Its financing and usage figures strengthen the commercial-traction case, but—as the cluster cautions—do not independently establish accuracy, productivity or intensive use, and the source offers little evidence on verification and governance.

kp.k: New funding targets agents and embedded legal engineering
kp.d: Harvey announced on 25 March 2026 that it raised $200 million at an $11 billion valuation, co-led by returning investors GIC and Sequoia. The company says the proceeds will expand customer-run agents and its global embedded legal engineering teams; CNBC reports the same intended uses. These are stated investment plans, rather than measured outcomes.
qs: Harvey, the legal infrastructure for law firms and in-house teams, today announced $200 million in new funding co-led by returning investors GIC and Sequoia.
The round values Harvey at $11 billion and includes participation from existing investors Andreessen Horowitz, Coatue, Conviction Partners, Elad Gil, Evantic, and Kleiner Perkins.
The investment will be used to expand the agents customers run on Harvey and grow the embedded legal engineering teams supporting them globally.

kp.k: Harvey claims agents increasingly execute complete legal workflows
kp.d: Harvey presents a shift from AI assistance toward agents carrying out high-volume and increasingly complex legal workflows from start to finish. CEO Winston Weinberg characterizes this as allowing lawyers to concentrate on judgment, strategy and outcomes. This is the vendor's account of changing task allocation, not a reported study of productivity or lawyer displacement.
qs: Legal work is undergoing a fundamental shift as high-volume and increasingly complex tasks move to AI agents that run workflows from start to finish.
Across law firms and corporate legal teams, work that once required significant manual effort is now carried out by agents.
AI isn’t just assisting lawyers. It’s becoming the system through which legal work gets done
The law firms and in-house teams leading the way are building agents that execute complex workflows so lawyers can focus on judgment, strategy, and outcomes.

kp.k: Custom agents extend into complex, long-duration legal work
kp.d: Harvey reports more than 25,000 custom agents operating across M&A, due diligence, contract drafting and document review. It says customers increasingly deploy long-horizon agents for extended, multi-step workflows such as fund formation, and use agents in Shared Spaces to coordinate legal teams and external partners. These are company-reported deployments and capabilities.
qs: More than 25,000 custom agents operate on Harvey, executing work across M&A, due diligence, contract drafting, and document review.
Customers are increasingly deploying long-horizon agents that handle multi-step workflows over extended periods for complex use cases such as fund formation.
They are also deploying agents within Shared Spaces to securely coordinate work across legal teams and their external partners.

kp.k: Legal engineers support customer-specific agent development
kp.d: Harvey describes legal engineers working alongside customers to build and continuously improve their agents. Separately, Sequoia partner Pat Grady argues in CNBC that rapid model improvements make real-world application a greater undertaking than for earlier software companies, requiring craft, taste and judgment. His explanation is an investor's view of implementation demands.
qs: Harvey’s legal engineers work alongside customers to build and continuously improve the agents that run their work.
Grady said that because model capabilities are improving so quickly, trying to apply them in real-world situations is a bigger undertaking than it has been for software companies in the past.
There's a lot of craft, taste and judgment that goes into determining how to use AI to achieve a particular job, he said.

kp.k: Reported adoption spans law firms and corporate buyers
kp.d: Harvey reports partnering with the majority of the AmLaw 100, over 500 in-house legal teams and 50 asset management firms across 60 countries, with more than 100,000 lawyers across 1,300 organizations using the platform. It names NBCUniversal and HSBC among recent customer wins, alongside expanded work with DLA Piper International and firmwide adoption at McCann Fitzgerald. CNBC explicitly attributes its user and organization counts to a release.
qs: The funding follows a period of rapid growth, with Harvey now partnering with the majority of the AmLaw 100, over 500 in-house legal teams, and 50 asset management firms across 60 countries.
Recent customer wins include NBCUniversal, HSBC, Corrs Chambers Westgarth, DLA Piper International expanding their work with Harvey, and McCann Fitzgerald going firmwide.
More than 100,000 lawyers across 1,300 organizations run their most important work on Harvey.

kp.k: Revenue and valuations indicate reported commercial expansion
kp.d: CNBC reports annual recurring revenue of $190 million in January, up from the $100 million figure announced in August. TechCrunch reports more than $1 billion in total funding and a valuation increase of over 3.5x in a year: $3 billion in February 2025, $5 billion in June, $8 billion in December and $11 billion in March 2026. These are commercial growth figures, distinct from evidence about legal-work quality or efficiency.
qs: The company hit $190 million in annual recurring revenue in January, up from the $100 million figure it announced in August.
With this new funding, the company has raised more than $1 billion in total, and its valuation jumped over 3.5x in a year.
Harvey was valued at $8 billion from a round announced in December, led by Andreessen Horowitz.
Before that, it was valued at $5 billion from a round led by Kleiner Perkins and Coatue, announced in June, and was at $3 billion from a Sequoia-led raise announced in February 2025.

kp.k: Industry specialization is presented as viable amid model competition
kp.d: CNBC frames Harvey as evidence that industry-focused AI startups can gain traction despite OpenAI and Anthropic expanding their offerings. Grady compares Harvey's AI-native application approach to Salesforce during the cloud transition. These are a journalistic interpretation and an investor analogy, rather than demonstrated conclusions about the long-term division of value between model companies and legal software vendors.
qs: Harvey is showing that AI startups focused on specific industries are able to get traction even as OpenAI and Anthropic continue expanding their offerings.
The company is among a growing crop of startups focused on deploying the latest AI technology in specialized and complex markets.
They sort of wrote the playbook for what it means to be an AI-native application company, which is the same thing Salesforce did back in the day with the cloud transition

kp.k: Leadership stresses adaptation; investors express long-term conviction
kp.d: Weinberg warns against complacency and predicts that relentlessly adapting companies will succeed as company-building changes. Grady describes Sequoia's repeated investment as an unusual demonstration of conviction and predicts Harvey could become one of the next decade's most important companies. These are strategic judgments and expectations from the CEO and an investor, not established future outcomes.
qs: I think any company right now, the worst mistake you can possibly do is become complacent, because how you build a company is completely changing
The companies that succeed are going to be the ones that are relentlessly adapting.
Co-leading three rounds in the same company is rare for Sequoia and reflects conviction that has only grown stronger since we first partnered at the Series A.
More than 100,000 lawyers around the world run their most critical work on Harvey, and we believe it's positioned to become one of the most important companies of the next decade.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Harvey Team and CEO Winston Weinberg describe a present shift from AI assistance toward agents executing legal workflows, with lawyers concentrating on judgment, strategy and outcomes.
pts.d: The Harvey announcement claims that agents already perform high-volume and increasingly complex legal work previously requiring substantial manual effort. Weinberg characterizes AI as becoming the system through which legal work is performed, rather than merely an assistant. Harvey Team identifies M&A, due diligence, contract drafting and document review as current applications, with increasing deployment of long-horizon agents for complex multi-step work such as fund formation. It also claims that Shared Spaces enables secure coordination across legal teams and external partners. These are company descriptions of deployment and capabilities, not independently measured findings about autonomy or output quality. The document does not specify whether outputs can be relied on without human verification.

pts.k: Ashley Capoot presents Harvey as evidence that industry-specific AI companies can gain traction despite expansion by foundation-model companies; investor Pat Grady predicts substantial long-term importance for Harvey.
pts.d: CNBC author Ashley Capoot frames Harvey's growth as demonstrating opportunities for specialized AI applications in complex markets despite concerns that OpenAI and Anthropic capture most AI industry value. Sequoia partner Pat Grady describes Harvey as a model for AI-native application businesses and, in the Harvey release, expresses belief that it could become one of the next decade's most important companies. These are respectively journalistic market interpretation and an investor's forecast. TechCrunch author Julie Bort characterizes Harvey as a major AI-era success and documents its financing trajectory, but offers no separate detailed prediction about changes to legal work.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists primarily of company-reported deployment figures, named customers, revenue growth and financing, supplemented by executive and investor statements.
pts.d: Harvey Team reports more than 25,000 custom agents, more than 100,000 lawyer users across 1,300 organizations, relationships with a majority of the AmLaw 100, over 500 in-house teams and 50 asset management firms across 60 countries. Named customers and expansions illustrate adoption rather than documented legal-work outcomes. CNBC explicitly attributes its user figures to the release and reports annual recurring revenue of $190 million in January, compared with $100 million announced in August. The three accounts report a $200 million round at an $11 billion valuation; TechCrunch supplies the earlier valuation sequence. These figures support the sources' growth narrative, while the workflow and lawyer-role claims rest on company descriptions and Weinberg's authority. Grady's forecast is an investor statement, with Sequoia's repeated investment offered as evidence of conviction. No benchmarks, measured time savings, comparative quality studies or detailed outcome cases are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Workflow changes are presented as already occurring by 25 March 2026; further agent expansion is planned without a deadline, while Grady's importance forecast extends over the next decade.
pts.d: All three pieces are dated 25 March 2026. Harvey's announcement uses present-tense deployment claims and describes long-horizon adoption as increasing, rather than predicting a specified date for universal adoption. Weinberg's account of lawyers shifting attention to judgment and strategy specifically concerns firms and in-house teams 'leading the way.' The funding is intended to expand agents and embedded legal engineering globally, but no rollout deadline or quantified target is given. In CNBC, Grady says rapidly improving model capabilities make real-world application demanding; Weinberg presents relentless adaptation as a condition for company success. The document gives no timetable for staffing reductions or profession-wide substitution.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed changes concern law firms, corporate legal departments and their external partners, with additional growth in legal engineering and the specialist legal-AI vendor market.
pts.d: Law firms and in-house teams are portrayed as moving manual workflow execution to agents while lawyers focus on judgment, strategy and outcomes. Adoption examples emphasize large firms, global enterprises and asset management organizations; the release also states a wider organizational footprint. External partners are affected through shared coordination tools. Harvey's legal engineers build and continuously improve customer agents, and their teams are to expand globally. Harvey is the software/platform vendor here, not an ALSP delivering legal services. The sources do not specify effects on associate headcount, junior training, billing arrangements, small-firm economics or access to justice.
